source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Expert reviewers blind-rated LLM-agent ideas as more novel than expert human ideas at the ideation stage.
numbers: 49 human ideas, 49 AI ideas, 49 AI ideas with human rerank; 79 reviewers, 298 unique reviews (N=104 people). Novelty 4.84 human, 5.64 AI, 5.81 AI+rerank (1-10); AI significantly higher, p<0.05, holds under multiple-test correction. Feasibility no significant difference.
limits: Ideas only, never run. NLP prompting topics. Style normalised by LLM; experts then guessed AI vs human at 50%.
agent_relevance: Novelty scores of unexecuted ideas are the thing later shown to be unreliable (see b05). Do not treat a high ideation novelty rating as a quality signal.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Human reviewers of ideas agree only a little: top/bottom 25% split-half consistency barely above chance.
numbers: Inter-reviewer consistency 56.1% (random 50%) on these ideas; NeurIPS 2021 reviewers 66.0%; ICLR 2024 (1.2K LLM submissions) 71.9%.
limits: Ideas without results are more subjective than papers. Split-half method with 20 random splits.
agent_relevance: Human novelty labels on bare ideas are a noisy ground truth. Any calibration set needs several raters and a reliability number.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Every LLM judge tested was at or below human-human agreement and near chance when ranking ideas.
numbers: Same balanced top/bottom 25% task: GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3 (best), AI Scientist reviewer agent 43.3; human 56.1.
limits: Models of 2024. On the ICLR accepted-vs-rejected pair task Claude-3.5 reached 71.4%, GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%.
agent_relevance: Supports G8: a model judge on ideas is near chance. Pairwise comparison beats direct scores but is still weak.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Reviewers' overall score tracks novelty and excitement, not feasibility.
numbers: Correlation with overall score: excitement r=0.854, novelty r=0.725, effectiveness 0.642, feasibility 0.097. Novelty vs feasibility r=-0.073.
limits: Correlations among reviewer ratings, not against truth.
agent_relevance: Novelty ratings carry a halo of overall liking. A novelty check should be separate from, and not stand in for, a feasibility check.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Executing the ideas reversed the AI advantage: expert-written ideas kept their scores, AI ideas fell.
numbers: 43 experts, over 100 hours each, 4-page papers, blind review. Score change after execution (1-10): human novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052, overall -0.628; AI novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879, overall -1.976. Differences in drops significant, FDR p=0.025 (novelty), 0.001, 0.003, 0.004.
quote: AI ideas' scores drop significantly more than human ideas
limits: N=43 projects. One field (NLP prompting). Executors were not the idea authors.
agent_relevance: Strongest warning against judging ideas by opinion. Execution outcome is the valid criterion; pre-execution novelty rating is not.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: After execution, the ranking of AI vs human ideas flipped on several metrics, but not significantly.
numbers: Excitement 3.90 AI vs 4.48 human; effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78. Not significant with N=43 ideas as independent points.
limits: Low power. Flip is suggestive only.
agent_relevance: Do not claim AI ideas are worse; claim the idea-stage rating failed to predict execution.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Ideation-stage scores barely predict execution-stage scores for the same ideas.
numbers: Pearson r, ideation vs execution: AI novelty -0.019, excitement -0.321, effectiveness 0.172, overall -0.092; human novelty -0.084, excitement 0.205, effectiveness 0.022, overall 0.158.
quote: the correlation is weak in most cases
limits: About 20 ideas per group. Different reviewers before and after.
agent_relevance: Predictive validity of the idea-stage rating is about zero. Use execution or a held-out test as the signal.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Reviewers of executed work consider more factors; empirical result and experiment rigor dominate.
numbers: Reviewer-comment coding into 10 categories; execution reviews cite empirical performance, experiment design, baselines and ablations far more than ideation reviews.
limits: Qualitative coding by the authors.
agent_relevance: Explains why execution beats judgment: results expose flaws that speculation misses. Gate ideas by a cheap run.

source: Falk et al. (2025) How Do Hackathons Foster Creativity? Towards AI Collaborative Evaluation of Creativity at Scale
finding: Human raters themselves agree poorly on novelty but better on usefulness.
numbers: 30 hackathon projects, 2 experienced raters, Cohen kappa novelty 0.18 (2 buckets) falling to 0.04 (5 levels); usefulness 0.53 falling to 0.12.
limits: Tiny sample (30). Kappa is absolute agreement, not rank consistency, and the authors say so.
agent_relevance: Novelty is the less reliable axis. Report agreement per axis and per granularity.

source: Falk et al. (2025) How Do Hackathons Foster Creativity? Towards AI Collaborative Evaluation of Creativity at Scale
finding: Small open LLM judges agree with humans variably; two LLMs agreed with each other at 0.59 on novelty.
numbers: 4 judges (Llama-3.1-8b, Mistral-7b, Gemma-2-9b, Prometheus-7b-v2) on 21,318 descriptions; novelty kappa Prometheus-Llama 0.59 (2 buckets); human 1 with Llama 0.42; usefulness best 0.46 (Mistral, Llama). Gemma gave score 3 about 80% of the time.
limits: Judges agree with each other more than with humans in places, which is a shared-bias risk. Models give optimistic, undifferentiated scores.
agent_relevance: LLM judges cluster in scale use. Rank-normalise scores. Agreement between judges is not validity (G4).

source: Falk et al. (2025) How Do Hackathons Foster Creativity? Towards AI Collaborative Evaluation of Creativity at Scale
finding: LLM judge text outputs were useful to humans as aids even when scores disagreed.
numbers: Raters scored judge explanations for representativeness and expert usefulness: Prometheus kappa 0.47 and 0.44; other models 0.05-0.2 and 0.20-0.30.
limits: Two raters. Judges sometimes invented project functions.
agent_relevance: Use the judge for retrieving prior art and giving reasons, not for the verdict.

source: Falk et al. (2025) How Do Hackathons Foster Creativity? Towards AI Collaborative Evaluation of Creativity at Scale
finding: Novelty is time-dependent: a project can lose novelty as similar ones appear.
numbers: Qualitative finding from rater discussion of 30 projects and the LLM outputs.
limits: Single study.
agent_relevance: A novelty test needs a dated prior-art corpus and should state the date.

source: Tutone, Franceschelli, Musolesi (2026) The Limits of Automatic Evaluation of Creativity in LLMs
finding: LLM judge strongly prefers AI-written stories; humans see no clear difference.
numbers: 200 WritingPrompts stories (100 human, 100 AI from 5 models), 11 dimensions. Human novelty 3.03 human vs 3.18 AI (p=.293); LLM novelty 4.90 vs 5.00 (p<.001). LLM gave a 5.00 ceiling to AI stories on several axes. Blind to source.
limits: One judge model family; stories, not ideas or code.
agent_relevance: Self-preference plus ceiling effect: never let the generator or a sibling model be the novelty judge (G8).

source: Tutone, Franceschelli, Musolesi (2026) The Limits of Automatic Evaluation of Creativity in LLMs
finding: LLM-human rank agreement on human stories is weak; surprise and novelty are not significant.
numbers: Kendall tau per dimension: elaboration 0.31 (p<.001, highest), creativity 0.23 (p=.007), novelty 0.10 (p=.224), surprise -0.01 (p=.867), usefulness 0.08 (p=.320), effectiveness 0.13 (p=.135).
limits: Dimension labels matched to tau values by reading the figure order.
agent_relevance: Surprise is the weakest-judged axis. Elaboration is the best-judged because it tracks length and detail.

source: Tutone, Franceschelli, Musolesi (2026) The Limits of Automatic Evaluation of Creativity in LLMs
finding: Automatic metrics have near-zero correlation with human creativity ratings.
numbers: Spearman rho mostly within -0.2 to 0.2: Creativity Index rho=0.07 with human creativity, at most 0.11 on any dimension; perplexity down to -0.23 (effectiveness) and -0.21 (elaboration); SBERT diversity negative.
limits: Negative trends mostly not significant. Short stories only.
agent_relevance: Raw distance or perplexity is not a stand-in for creativity: more divergence was rated worse when coherence broke. Need novelty AND value.

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
finding: An LLM judge with a rubric and the run history matched human novelty labels best among automatic methods.
numbers: 300 episodes, 3 trained annotators, ordinal Krippendorff alpha 0.724. Spearman vs humans: GPT-5 0.732 [0.675,0.781], GLM-5 0.703, DeepSeek V3.2 0.700, Qwen3-235B 0.685, GPT-OSS-120B 0.544; semantic nearest neighbour 0.637, centroid 0.589, mean 0.503, graph -0.329; concept set membership 0.508.
limits: Novelty is relative to the agent's own earlier episodes in code tasks, with an anchored rubric (Boden levels 0-4). Not absolute novelty against the literature.
agent_relevance: Key boundary: comparative, anchored, code-grounded novelty can be judged well; absolute novelty of prose ideas cannot. Our agent should judge change against its own previous attempts.

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
finding: The good judge result was robust to prompt ablation and showed no self-preference or verbosity bias in this setting.
numbers: Leave-one-out Spearman: full 0.732, no examples 0.684, no edge rules 0.699, no procedure 0.712. GPT-5 scored Qwen episodes higher than its own (+0.300 vs +0.129 relative to a DeepSeek judge, p=0.000038). Length partial correlation near zero.
limits: Only 3 biases tested, on 10 MLE-Bench tasks.
agent_relevance: Anchor examples help (0.684 without). Run a cross-model self-preference check as a standard test.

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks
finding: Novelty and usefulness are decoupled in agent runs: more novelty did not give better scores.
numbers: Spearman of per-episode change in impact vs change in P-creativity: human -0.111 (p<0.05), AIDE GPT-5 -0.021, AIDE Qwen3-32B 0.056, AIRA -0.026. Strategic exploration 75% of behaviour early, 25% by end of run.
limits: Kaggle-style tasks; 10 tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports a separate value check. Novelty without a test is not progress; agents also decay to exploitation.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning
finding: A stratified LLM novelty scorer reaches human-expert-like agreement on idea novelty, but only moderate.
numbers: Against 98 ideas (49 AI, 49 human) from Si et al. 2024: Spearman 0.358 median, 0.411 mean, 0.427 min, 0.245 max aggregation; binary accuracy 0.602/0.633/0.469/0.612 vs human-human 0.571. MAD to individual raters 1.70 vs human-human 1.73 (N=91). Agentic Reviewer reference: human-human 0.41, LLM-human 0.42.
quote: scores disagree with individual human experts no more than human experts disagree with each other
limits: Compared to aggregated human score, which favours the LLM. Authors' own scorer.
agent_relevance: Human-human noise is the ceiling; a stratified scorer reaches it, no further. Our novelty test may be only about 0.4 in rank agreement.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning
finding: Human pairwise preference for novelty has only moderate agreement.
numbers: Analogy-method solutions chosen as more novel 78% of the time; inter-annotator kappa 0.445. Reasonableness 67%.
limits: Pairwise, forced choice, small panel.
agent_relevance: Pairwise human labels are more reliable than scalar ones; use pairwise for calibration sets.

source: Sawicki et al. (2025) Can LLMs Outperform Non-Experts in Poetry Evaluation? CAT
finding: LLMs using forced-choice ranking in small batches beat non-expert humans at ranking poems by true venue quality.
numbers: 90-poem set (Lamb et al. 2015), ground truth publication venue. Claude-3-Opus Spearman 0.87 (best, 15 poems per prompt, rank-derived score) vs best non-expert human 0.38 (novelty). ICC across 10 runs 0.9-0.99. Whole 90-poem prompt: 0.57-0.62.
limits: Possible training-data contamination of published poems; one domain; batch size matters (90 at once is worse).
agent_relevance: Method matters: ranking in small batches, repeated runs, rank-derived scores. Averaging runs gives reliability.

source: Sawicki et al. (2025) Can LLMs Outperform Non-Experts in Poetry Evaluation? CAT
finding: Non-expert human judges inverted the quality ground truth, except on novelty.
numbers: Lamb et al. 2015 non-experts (as reported by Sawicki): Quality SRC -0.33, Skill -0.35, Wellbeing -0.45, Effort -0.45; Novelty +0.38 the only positive.
limits: Re-analysis of old data, not a new human study.
agent_relevance: Lay ratings can be anti-correlated with expert quality. Novelty was the one axis laypeople got right.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or Artifice? LLMs and the False Promise of Creativity (TTCW)
finding: Experts agree moderately on single binary tests but strongly in aggregate (CAT-style).
numbers: 10 writers, 48 stories, 2,016 binary judgments, 3 independent evaluations per story. Fleiss kappa per test 0.27-0.66, mean 0.41; Pearson on number of tests passed 0.69.
limits: Short stories; one profession; paid experts.
agent_relevance: Aggregating many binary tests raises reliability. Use many cheap checks instead of one holistic score.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or Artifice? LLMs and the False Promise of Creativity (TTCW)
finding: LLM stories pass far fewer expert creativity tests than professional ones.
numbers: LLM-written stories passed 3-10 times fewer TTCW tests than New Yorker stories; GPT-3.5 stories ranked least preferred about two-thirds of the time.
limits: 48 stories; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: The gap was measured by experts, not LLM judges.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or Artifice? LLMs and the False Promise of Creativity (TTCW)
finding: LLM judges administering the same tests did not correlate with experts.
numbers: Cohen kappa averages across 14 tests: GPT-3.5 0.016, GPT-4 0.035, Claude v1.3 -0.006; best single test GPT-4 originality in thought 0.31. Few-shot on a couple of tests gave no gain.
quote: none of the LLMs positively correlate with the expert assessments
limits: Long-form stories; 2023 models; zero-shot prompts.
agent_relevance: Boundary: long holistic text is the weakest case for LLM judges. Anchored, short comparisons work better (b17).

source: Grouchnikov, Gregory, Noh (2026) Poly-Encoders for Automated Creativity Assessment
finding: Fine-tuned small encoders match fine-tuned LLMs in scoring divergent-thinking responses.
numbers: 18,000 SCTT responses with human ratings; poly-encoder Pearson up to r=0.74 [0.73,0.75]; LLaMA-2-7b fine-tune 0.74; GPT-3/T5 on 27,217 AUT responses up to 0.81; GPT-4 zero-shot 0.2-0.67 across studies. Human rater w=0.85, test-retest r=0.67.
limits: Label noise; same-task training, so generalisation to new tasks is untested.
agent_relevance: Task-specific trained scorers reach 0.74-0.81; zero-shot LLMs vary 0.2-0.67. Human test-retest 0.67 caps what to expect.

source: Domanti et al. (2026) The Effect of Idea Elaboration on Automatic Assessment of Idea Originality
finding: Automatic originality scorers favour machine text, and the bias shrinks when response elaboration is controlled.
numbers: 4,813 AUT responses (3,548 ChatGPT-4o, 1,265 from 81 humans), 2 expert coders blind to source; scorers OCSAI, CLAUS, ChatGPT-4o. ChatGPT-4o mean originality of its own responses fell 1.43 points (3.49 to 2.06) when only the core idea was scored.
limits: Humans split into higher and lower creative groups: high-creative humans beat machine core ideas. One task (AUT: shoe, fork).
agent_relevance: Length or elaboration inflates automatic originality scores. Judge a normalised core idea, not the full text (matches G5 length normalisation).

source: Domanti et al. (2026) The Effect of Idea Elaboration on Automatic Assessment of Idea Originality
finding: A prior elaboration bias in OCSAI was replicated with core-idea scoring.
numbers: Core-idea control reduced the machine advantage in OCSAI, CLAUS and ChatGPT-4o; OCSAI effect only marginally significant for higher-creative humans.
limits: Builds on Arora et al. and Tang et al. (cited, not opened).
agent_relevance: A cheap fix exists: extract and score the core idea only.

source: Sawicki et al. (2025) Can LLMs Outperform Non-Experts in Poetry Evaluation? CAT
finding: Cited background: GPT-4 judgments reached over 80% agreement with human consensus on chatbot quality.
numbers: Zheng et al. 2023, as quoted in Sawicki et al.
limits: Cited only; not opened. Chat helpfulness, not creativity.
agent_relevance: Do not transfer agreement on helpfulness to novelty.
